passages.text: ‘After leaving here yesterday, friends, I confess that I could not sleep, so concerned was I about the inquiry that was to take place with Apion. While I lay awake, what I had contrived against him in Rome came rushing into my mind. It was as follows. From childhood I, Clement, loved truth and sought what mattered to the soul, spending my time on refutations and demonstrations but unable to find anything conclusive. Through brooding I drifted into illness. While I was lying sick, Apion came to Rome. He was a friend of my father's and stayed as my guest. On learning that I was bedridden, he came in to me, being not uninitiated in medicine, and asked the reason for my confinement to bed. But I, knowing that this man held the Jews in intense hatred, to the point of writing many books against them, and that even now he welcomed Simon into friendship not from love of learning, but because he knew him to be a Samaritan who hated Jews and had come forward against them—for this reason he had drawn Simon close, so that he might learn something from him against the Jews—’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired terms concern dismantling and establishing arguments. Both sides of the inquiry are retained, rather than reducing the activity to criticism alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῆς συνοίας ἐξώκειλα εἰς νόσον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Through brooding I drifted into illness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The mental preoccupation is connected with illness, and the movement verb retains a faint drifting or running-aground image. Dejection or anxious reflection are material alternatives to brooding; no medical diagnosis is inferred.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He was a friend of my father's
lexical_decisions.rationale: The inherited or paternal friendship is rendered through the father, not as a claim that Apion was Clement's biological father.
The litotes and initiation image are retained. The phrase indicates some medical knowledge without certifying professional qualification.

passages.text: ‘Knowing these things beforehand about Apion, as soon as he asked the cause of the illness, I answered in pretense, “I am suffering what young people suffer, and my soul is in pain.” He said, “My child, take courage and speak to me as to a father: what is your soul's illness?” I again sighed in pretense, as though ashamed to speak about love, and by my silence and downward nodding gave him the suspicion of what I wished to suggest. Truly persuaded that I was in love with a woman, he said, “There is nothing in life for which help cannot be found. For when I was young, I too fell in love with a most distinguished woman. I thought not only that it was impossible to obtain her, but had no hope even of ever greeting her. Yet I met an Egyptian very thoroughly versed in the arts of magicians, became his friend, and disclosed my love. He not only put himself at my disposal for everything I wanted, but, showing still greater generosity toward me, did not begrudge teaching me the incantation through which I succeeded. Persuaded by the generosity of my teacher through his secret instruction, and having succeeded once, I ceased from love.”’

lexical_decisions.rationale: Both occurrences make Clement's performance explicitly feigned. The translation does not present the supposed romantic illness as an authentic disclosure.
The superlative concerns being worthy of regard or mention, not expressly physical beauty. Most remarkable is a material alternative; beautiful would add a characteristic not supplied here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the incantation through which I succeeded
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source reports an incantation but does not provide its words or method in this passage. The English neither invents a spell nor claims independent efficacy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having succeeded once, I ceased from love
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the single success and the ensuing cessation of love are retained. The statement is not rewritten into continued passion or an unexpressed permanent relationship.

passages.text: For just as fearsome snakes draw sparrows to themselves by their breath, so these beings draw those sharing their table toward their own will, mingling with their minds through food and drink. They transform themselves in dreams into the forms of carved images in order to increase deception. For the carved image is neither alive nor possessed of a divine spirit; the demon that appeared made use of its form. To how many other people have they similarly appeared in dreams, and, when those people met one another while awake and compared what they had seen in dreams, did not agree? Thus that is no longer a dream apparition, but is either a demon's appearance or the soul's, giving images in response to the fears and desire that arise. For, struck in mind by fear, it brings forth images through dreams. If you think that carved images, being possessed of breath, can perform such things, set them on a balance. With the beam level, place the counterweight on the other pan, and ask them to become either heavier or lighter. If that happens, they have breath. But it does not happen. If it does, is such a thing thereby a god? For this can happen even by a demon's finger. Worms move too, and are not called gods.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The snake comparison uses breath or exhalation, not a separate snake spirit. The ensuing mingling of demons with minds is retained as the speaker's ancient explanatory claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥστε οὐκέτι ὄναρ ἐπιφανείη ἐκεῖνό ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus that is no longer a dream apparition
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual form ἐπιφανείη is taken nominally as apparition or manifestation alongside the copula ἐστιν. An optative verbal reading, might appear, is morphologically possible but does not fit this copular sequence readily. No divine adjective absent from the clause is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ ἔσται, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: If it does, is such a thing thereby a god?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following demon-finger and worm counterexamples support a rhetorical challenge rather than an affirmation of divinity. The Greek clause can formally be read as an assertion; the rhetorical-question punctuation is interpretive and disclosed, not a change to the words.
The two weight alternatives govern the balance test. No modern measurement, physical explanation, or successful experimental result is supplied.

source_issues.issue: The supplied form παρίᾳ has no defensible clear meaning or agreement established in this construction. The draft renders the surrounding fears, desire, and images but leaves this word's contribution unresolved; that is an incomplete rendering, not an emendation or a claim of full coverage. Source-level or scholarly resolution is required before publication.

passages.text: How many also falsely claim oracular responses and cures accomplished by these images, and confirm them with oaths? How many have hired themselves out, undertaking through certain contrivances to suffer something and proclaiming it in this way, then, having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment, say that the cure was revealed by an oracle, so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship? How many of these objects were consecrated from the beginning by magical art, so that they might give oracles? Yet over a long time these too proved discordant. How many now practice sorcery, wishing to strengthen such things? Nevertheless, if something has powers of divination or healing, that does not make it a god.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive restoration concerns the people in respect of their affliction; the affliction itself is not restored or strengthened. The counteraction opposes the contrived affliction. Its exact technique is not given, so no substance, remedy, or procedure is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The insensate thing is the object labeled, with object of worship its assigned designation. The claim of an oracular cure is being used to confer that designation; the main text does not invent an actual written dedication.

lexical_decisions.chosen: over a long time these too proved discordant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The loss of agreement or reliability is retained without inventing a particular failed oracle or a quantitative error rate.

source_issues.issue: The supplied verb ὑνερπολῇ has no defensible lexical rendering established here. The draft translates the following giving of oracles but does not claim to have translated this first coordinated action. It has not silently substituted an unprinted form or invented a dotted gap. The unresolved word blocks publication until source-level or scholarly resolution.
